description: An editorial guide to the seven concepts, with source-section excerpts and explicit interpretive boundaries.

concepts.title: Semantic Participation
concepts.question: Under which conditions does a generated output qualify as an artifact in a structured environment?
concepts.summary: Specifies the environment, alignment, validation status, epistemic type, dependencies and permitted use of a candidate artifact.

concepts.title: Typed Generativity
concepts.question: Which target object is being requested, and what constitutes a candidate inhabitant?
concepts.summary: Separates target-type inference, constraint extraction, candidate construction and validity checks.

concepts.title: Functorial Consistency
concepts.question: Do corresponding source-side and target-side transformations satisfy a declared agreement relation?
concepts.summary: Introduces a typed two-path evaluation item with explicit equivalence regimes, independent adequacy checks and failure labels.

concepts.title: Lambek Machines
concepts.question: Does explicit typed composition improve controlled evaluation of linguistic meaning?
concepts.summary: Uses linguistic composition and controlled transformation tests as domain-specific hypotheses, with explicit empirical conditions.

concepts.title: Algebraic Architectures
concepts.question: Which structural commitments should a model architecture satisfy for a specified task?
concepts.summary: Treats architecture choice as a testable specification of object types, transformations, invariants and predicted failure modes.

concepts.title: Quantitative Curry–Howard
concepts.question: What does a numerical score establish about a typed candidate artifact?
concepts.summary: Records the target of quantitative evidence, calibration, validation status, uncertainty and permitted inference without equating a score with proof.

concepts.title: Effectful and Conceptual Intelligence
concepts.question: Under which authority and effect constraints does an artifact enter consequential execution?
concepts.summary: Distinguishes a candidate plan from authorized execution, validated state change and controlled conceptual transfer.

relations.label: Membership criteria motivate the specification of target types and candidate inhabitants.

evidence.excerpt: Essay 1 defines the membership criterion for the series. Essay 2 analyzes target-type inference and candidate construction.
Typed Generativity converts the external standard of Semantic Participation into an internal diagnostic for generation.

relations.scope: The essays define a conceptual sequence. They do not claim that every generative implementation performs a membership check before producing a candidate.

relations.label: Candidate construction leads to the proposed transformation-sensitive evaluation.

evidence.excerpt: Essay 3 then tests whether the generated object changes correctly under structured transformations.
Functorial Consistency then tests whether the candidate artifact maintains the relation that connects it to source transformations and target operations.

relations.scope: An item-level transformation test applies only if the two paths, typed outputs, comparison relation, and independent adequacy checks are specified.

relations.label: The two-path framework is proposed for controlled linguistic transformations.

evidence.excerpt: The source side can vary paraphrase, quantifier scope, attachment, lexical choice, or representation format
Functorial Language Consistency instantiates the two-path benchmark for a declared linguistic transformation f and semantic representation.

relations.scope: The linguistic benchmark is a proposed domain instantiation; the cited sections report no improvement from an implemented model.

relations.label: Transformation obligations inform task-specific architecture specifications.

evidence.excerpt: An architecture extension must state which task transformations a model family supports.
ArchitectureSpec inherits the transformation requirement from Functorial Consistency.

relations.scope: Architecture-level preservation commitments depend on task-specific transformation classes. The connection establishes a design obligation, not a guarantee of model behavior.

relations.label: The linguistic instantiation motivates general questions about architecture choice.

evidence.excerpt: Essay 4 prepares the architecture-level question by isolating a case in which task structure is explicit.
The language layer instantiates these ideas in typed linguistic composition.

relations.scope: The linguistic case motivates architectural questions. The cited sections do not establish a performance benefit from a particular architecture.

relations.label: Architecture specifications lead to separate questions about quantitative evidence.

evidence.excerpt: Architecture determines which structures a model represents and which validators it exposes
Quantitative Curry-Howard supplies the evidence layer for candidate typed artifacts.

relations.scope: Architecture specifications and quantitative evidence records serve different purposes. Numerical evidence needs its own estimand, validation target, and calibration basis.

relations.label: Quantitative warrant is an input to action authorization, never a substitute for it.

evidence.excerpt: quantitative warrant becomes an input to authorization and audit.
Scores, validators, and epistemic types guide action only through an authorization surface

relations.scope: Evidence concerning a proposed action and authorization to execute it remain separate decisions, with distinct validators and authority conditions.

relations.label: Consequential action remains subject to environment-relative admission and permitted-use conditions.

evidence.excerpt: The suite converges on a single evaluation object: typed artifacts in structured environments, with validation, transformation stability, warrant, and effect control.

relations.scope: This is a cross-cutting applicability constraint, not a chronological feedback step, a mathematical implication, or evidence that any deployed system satisfies the membership criterion.
